pinterest.title: Indonesian Wedding Traditions: Ten Customs and the Communities They Belong To
pinterest.description: There is no single Indonesian wedding. Indonesian wedding traditions belong to particular communities and faiths: the Javanese siraman and panggih, the akad nikah of a Muslim wedding, the Balinese Hindu pawiwahan, the Minangkabau suntiang, the Batak ulos, and Bugis and Makassar customs before the wedding. Each custom is tied only to the group its sources name. Plus what makes a wedding in Bali legal for Australians.

pinterest.title: Javanese Wedding Traditions: Siraman, Midodareni and Panggih Explained
pinterest.description: Javanese wedding traditions run as a sequence across more than one day. Siraman is a ritual bath for both bride and groom, meant to cleanse them outwardly and inwardly. Midodareni is held on the night before the core rites. Panggih is the meeting of bride and groom once they are legally married. Read the Kraton Yogyakarta's account of its royal weddings, and why elders who pour the siraman water need to arrive a day or two early.

pinterest.title: Balinese Wedding Traditions: The Pawiwahan as a Sacred Rite of Purification
pinterest.description: A Balinese Hindu wedding, the pawiwahan, is a sacred rite that binds a man and woman as husband and wife through purification of body and spirit. An academic study sets out the order, from an auspicious day chosen by the Balinese calendar to the purification rite. Practice differs between villages and families, and these rites belong with a priest and the family, not on a reception programme. Thinking of getting married in Bali? The guide also covers what makes it legal.

slides: There is no single Indonesian wedding. Ten customs, and the communities they belong to.
Javanese: siraman, a ritual bath for bride and groom, then midodareni, the night before the core rites.
Muslim weddings: the akad nikah, where the ijab qobul vow is spoken. The offer, then the acceptance.
Balinese Hindu: the pawiwahan is a sacred rite of purification. It belongs with a priest and the family, not on a reception programme.
West Sumatra: the suntiang, a gold-coloured, many-tiered headdress worn by the Minangkabau bride.
North Sumatra: the ulos, the woven cloth of the Batak. Giving it, mangulosi, is a sign of blessing.
Marrying in Bali? Australians need a Certificate of No Impediment, a shared recognised religion and proper registration. Check every step with the embassy and the registry.
Honouring a partner's family or drawn to Bali? Begin the conversation with a Wedded Advisor.
instagram_carousel.caption:
There is no single Indonesian wedding. A Javanese family, a Muslim couple, a Balinese Hindu household, a Minangkabau, Batak or Bugis clan will each mark a marriage in their own way.

Our guide to Indonesian wedding traditions takes ten customs and ties each one only to the group its sources name. Some details are recorded by a royal palace or a university journal. Others are simply often told, and we say so.

A few things worth knowing:
Siraman, the Javanese flower bath, falls before the core rites, so elders who pour the water need to arrive a day or two early.
A Balinese purification belongs with a priest, an akad nikah with an imam or the KUA.
Batik, the Minangkabau suntiang and the Batak ulos each carry meaning for a specific community and are best worn or given with that family's guidance.

If one of you is Indonesian or Indonesian-Australian, the right version of a custom is your family's version. Ask parents and elders which rites matter and who should lead them.

Planning to marry in Bali? The guide covers the Certificate of No Impediment, religion and registration, as general information, not legal advice.

Read the full guide via the link in our bio. And when you would like to talk your plans through, send us a message to speak with a Wedded Advisor.
